title: Accordion: origami-fold one thinned wafer into an 8-tier stack
idea: Random stimulus 'accordion' forced onto stacking: build a planar DRAM array on a wafer thinned to ~5 um on a polyimide carrier, leaving 200 um flexible RDL 'hinge' strips between array panels, then fold the strip like bellows so 8 panels stack face-to-back. Bitline and I/O buses run continuously through the hinges, so the stack needs no TSVs and no per-layer bonding.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6) and per-layer bond yield: no TSV keep-out and no die-to-die alignment; claim wafer area per stacked bit -30 to -50% versus HBM, and lower capital per stacked GB.

title: Honeycomb: three line families at 120 degrees with active back-gate shields
idea: Forced connection to a honeycomb: put vertical-channel cells on a hex lattice with three line families at 0, 60 and 120 degrees: wordlines, bitlines, and a third family of back-gate 'shield lines'. When a wordline fires, the shield lines that cross its neighbors pulse negative to hold their channels hard off, and hex packing gives about 15% more capacitor footprint than a square grid.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) and capacitor wall (fact 1): neighbors are actively clamped during aggressor activations, aiming at a ~10x flip threshold; +15% capacitor footprint per cell.

title: Skyscraper sky lobby: sense-amp tier every 16 cell tiers
idea: Like express elevators that feed sky lobbies, a 128-tier vertical-bitline 3D DRAM inserts a layer-transferred single-crystal Si sense-amp tier every 16 cell tiers. Each local vertical bitline spans only 16 cells, and sensed data rides 'express' global vertical lines down to the base die.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2) and capacitor wall (fact 1): bitline capacitance per sense ~8x lower, so a 1-1.5 fF lateral capacitor gives the signal of today's 5 fF pillar, which makes lateral 3D capacitors good enough.

title: Sushi conveyor: vertical charge-packet shift string replaces per-cell capacitors
idea: Forced connection to a sushi belt: in a NAND-like stack of 64 gate tiers around a low-leakage IGZO or poly-Si vertical channel, bits are stored as charge packets in gate-induced potential wells and clocked along the string CCD-style to one sense node at the base. There is no capacitor or access transistor per bit, only a gate electrode over a shared channel, and reads stream in order like plates passing a diner.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2): bit cost tracks NAND-like tier cost (claim ~5-10x below 2D DRAM at 64+ tiers) with unlimited endurance; latency 20-70 ns by position, suited to streaming rows such as KV caches.

title: Pin-art toy: alignment-free bonding onto an unpatterned nano-capacitor forest
idea: Like a pin-art toy taking any shape, make a separate capacitor wafer as an unpatterned forest of isolated 8 nm-pitch nanopillar capacitors (separate bottom electrodes, common top plate), then hybrid-bond it to the transistor wafer. Each ~20 nm landing pad touches 4-6 pillars in parallel while pillars over the gaps touch nothing, so the capacitor needs no mask and zero overlay to the cells.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1) and litho capital (fact 4): the critical capacitor-hole EUV layer disappears and capacitors come from a cheap separate fab; claim -1 to -2 EUV layers and ~10% lower wafer cost.

title: Bamboo nodes: two-deck capacitor stitched at a conductive landing node
idea: Bamboo grows tall in segments joined at nodes: etch the capacitor hole as two ~45:1 decks with a TiN landing 'node' and SiN support ring between them, as 3D NAND does for two-deck channel holes, then form the electrode and dielectric continuously through both decks. The effective aspect ratio reaches ~90-110:1 without one extreme etch.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1, needs AR ~115): ~1.6-2x capacitor area, so Cs 8-10 fF or today's Cs at a smaller F.

title: Velcro: press-fit nanowire forests make stacked memory dies reworkable
idea: Forced connection to hook-and-loop: grow 2 um Cu nanowire or CNT forests on both die faces at 10 um pad pitch, so dies interlock by room-temperature press-fit with low contact resistance. A die that fails stack test is pulled and replaced before the final anneal and underfill lock the stack.
why: HBM stack yield loss of 20-30% (fact 6) becomes rework: claim stack yield ~70% to ~95% and cost per HBM bit about -20%.

title: Tree rings: concentric ALD shells store three bits per hole
idea: Like growth rings in a trunk, fill one wide high-AR hole with alternating storage and plate shells (TiN/ZrO2/TiN/ZrO2/TiN...). Each storage shell surfaces at a different radius on a terraced top and wires to its own access transistor, so one etched hole holds 2-3 coaxial capacitors.
why: Capacitor wall and litho (facts 1, 4): 2-3x fewer holes per bit; wide holes at relaxed pitch move the critical capacitor litho from EUV to DUV.

title: Iceberg: bitlines built from the wafer backside under 4F2 cells
idea: Most of an iceberg is underwater: build a 4F2 vertical-channel array with capacitors on the front, bond to a carrier, thin to the channel bottoms, and form low-resistance Cu or Ru bitlines on the backside, the way logic now does backside power. No buried bitline has to survive the full front-end thermal budget.
why: Litho-bound scaling (fact 4): makes 4F2 practical, a cell 33% smaller than 6F2, without buried-bitline resistance or thermal limits; claim ~30% more bits per wafer at the same F.

title: Bookshelf: dies stand on edge, bonded spine-down onto logic
idea: Books stand spine-out on a shelf: dice 30 um DRAM dies, polish one edge to expose bitline and I/O wires routed there, then stand 100+ dies upright and hybrid-bond their edges onto a logic base die. Each edge carries thousands of wires at ~2 um pitch, and no die needs a TSV.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6) and data movement (fact 5): no TSV area or yield loss, one base die hosts 100+ dies with short uniform wires; claim ~1 pJ/bit and TB-class stacks.

title: Rubik's cube: transposable 3D cell with orthogonal row and column access
idea: A Rubik's cube twists along either axis: each storage node connects to two access transistors in different tiers, a lower one gated by an X-wordline onto Y-bitlines and an upper one gated by a Y-wordline onto X-bitlines. The array can open a row or a column, so matrix transposes and column-wise tensor reads need no overfetch.
why: Overfetch (fact 8) and data movement (fact 5): claim 2-4x less energy per useful bit on transposed or strided AI access, at ~1.3x cell area that tiers absorb.

title: Three-way road junction: sense amps shared by three hexagonal mats
idea: Forced connection from a three-way junction: tile the die with hexagonal mats so each sense-amp cluster sits where three mats meet, and multiplex one sense amp across bitlines from three mats instead of the two of open-bitline sharing. Sub-wordline drivers line the hex edges and serve the two mats on either side.
why: Periphery is 49% of the die (fact 7): one-third fewer sense amps per bit; claim periphery ~49% to ~40% of the die and ~15% more bits per wafer.

title: Coral reef: self-ordered anodic alumina pores as capacitor molds
idea: Coral builds its skeleton bottom-up: deposit ~1.5 um of Al over the transistor array, pre-dimple it at each storage-node landing pad, and anodize it. Self-organized pores grow straight down from the dimples at aspect ratios beyond 100:1, and lining them with TiN/ZrO2/TiN makes the capacitors with no high-AR plasma etch.
why: Capacitor wall and capital (facts 1, 4): AR >100:1 from wet electrochemistry; claim capacitor-module capex -50% and Cs ~8 fF.

title: Lotus-leaf droplets: capillary self-assembly bonds memory tiles onto logic
idea: Water beads align on a lotus leaf: put a droplet on each hydrophilic bond site of a logic wafer, release thousands of small (1-2 mm2) known-good DRAM tiles in fluid, and let surface tension pull each tile to <0.5 um alignment before it direct-bonds as the water evaporates. No fine-alignment die-to-wafer bonder is needed.
why: 3D integration capital and throughput (facts 4, 6): batch fluidic placement at >10k tiles/hour replaces $10M+ D2W bonders, making memory-on-logic cheap.

title: Puff pastry: exponential lamination reaches 128 tiers in seven bonds
idea: Fold-and-roll multiplies pastry layers exponentially: build a 2-tier single-crystal cell stack, bond it face-down onto an identical stack and split off the donor to get 4 tiers, then repeat 4-on-4 and 8-on-8. 128 tiers take 7 bonding steps instead of 128 depositions, and every tier keeps a single-crystal channel.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2): single-crystal lateral transistors far beyond the 26-tier breakeven with log2 process steps; claim cost per bit -40% versus 2D.

title: Venetian blinds: slanted overlapping plate capacitors cut by angled ion beam
idea: Blind slats overlap one another: angled ion-beam etching at 45-60 degrees cuts slanted trenches so each cell's plate capacitor leans over its neighbors' footprint like overlapping slats. Plate area reaches 3-4x the cell footprint with only a ~20:1 vertical etch.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): ~5 fF at ~3x lower vertical aspect ratio, so pillar toppling and etch-tool limits relax.

title: Kitchen sponge: gyroid block-copolymer electrode fills each capacitor well
idea: A sponge hides huge internal surface: spin a gyroid-forming block copolymer into each capacitor well, remove one block, and ALD-coat the continuous 3D network with TiN/high-k/TiN so the electrode becomes a triply periodic minimal surface. At a 20-25 nm period the internal area is about 10x that of a plain cylinder.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): 5 fF at AR ~15:1, or 20+ fF at today's aspect ratio for much longer retention.

title: Piano keys: staggered-height checkerboard capacitors double each level's pitch
idea: Black keys sit higher than white keys: in a checkerboard, even cells' capacitors start on the landing-pad layer while odd cells' capacitors start one level up on a conductive riser. Each level then holds capacitors at 1.41x the lateral pitch with about 2x the cross-section each.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): ~2x storage cross-section at the same density, or the same Cs in a ~25% smaller cell.

title: Swiss roll: strained nanomembranes self-roll into capacitor scrolls
idea: A Swiss roll packs a long sheet into a small volume: deposit a planar TiN/HZO/TiN/HZO multilayer on a strained SiGe/Si bilayer in each lateral 3D cell, then release it with a selective etch so it curls into a 4-5 turn scroll inside the cell recess. Plate area grows with sheet length rather than etch depth.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2): flat lateral capacitors give <1 fF; scrolls could give 5-10 fF in a 200 nm recess.

title: Chessboard: alternating NMOS and PMOS access rows neutralize row hammer
idea: Black and white squares alternate: alternate n-channel and p-channel access transistors (storing opposite logic polarity) row by row, so an aggressor's wordline swings opposite to its neighbors' turn-on polarity. Its capacitive kick pushes the victims further off, and the electron-injection mechanism behind hammer flips works against p-type neighbors.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): aiming at a >10x higher flip threshold (1k to 10k+ activations); coupling is cancelled at the source rather than mitigated by refresh logic.

title: Sourdough starter: one reusable donor wafer seeds every single-crystal tier
idea: Keep one starter and bake many loaves: grow porous-Si plus epi-Si on a premium Czochralski donor, split off a 50 nm single-crystal layer for each 3D DRAM tier, then re-polish and regrow the donor 10-20 times. Each stacked tier uses only a fraction of a newly pulled wafer.
why: Scarce resources: Spruce Pine quartz crucibles (>80%) and CZ wafer supply; claim ~10x fewer pulled wafers per tier, plus thin, high-quality channels for 3D (fact 2).

title: Hairpin: U-turn vertical channel puts both cell terminals on top
idea: Bend the channel like a hairpin: etch a narrow slot in each 4F2 cell and line it with a U-shaped Si or oxide-semiconductor channel around a core gate, so source and drain both land on top and the bitline and capacitor contacts sit side by side above the cell. The channel is twice the slot depth long, which keeps leakage low, in a 4F2 footprint with no buried bitline.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3) and 4F2 scaling (fact 4): ~100 nm effective channel in 4F2; claim a 10x lower leakage tail (4-8x longer refresh interval).

title: Lighthouse: infrared beams through silicon replace TSV fields between dies
idea: Silicon is transparent at 1310 nm the way air is to a lighthouse beam: put micro-LED or VCSEL emitters and Ge photodiodes at matching metal-free windows on thinned stacked dies, so each link beams straight through several dies to its receiver. Hundreds of wide optical channels replace thousands of TSVs and their keep-out zones.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): no metal vias through cell dies; claim 10-15% less die area per bit and +10 points stack yield, at ~1 pJ/bit link energy.

title: Ship in a bottle: cell wafer bonded onto 28nm periphery wafer
idea: Build the ship outside, then slide it in: make a cell-only wafer (arrays, bitline sense amps and local column mux in the cell process) and a separate periphery wafer in a mature 28 nm logic fab carrying decoders, data paths and the standard DDR5 PHY, then wafer-to-wafer hybrid bond at ~0.5 um pitch with one bond per 16 bitlines. The bonded die is a normal DDR5 x8 part with the same pinout, commands and timing.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7) and EUV capital (fact 4): cell-wafer area per bit about -40%, and periphery moves to depreciated U.S. 28 nm fabs (U.S. manufacturability).

title: Kangaroo pouch: spare-subarray chiplet carried beside the HBM base die
idea: A pouch carries a spare: co-package a small 'spare' DRAM chiplet bonded under or beside the HBM base die, and give the base die a CAM that redirects any failed core-die subarray to spare subarrays within the tRCD budget. Hosts see a standard HBM3E stack, and failures found after stacking are repaired instead of scrapped.
why: HBM yield loss of 20-30% (fact 6): claim stack yield above 90% and cost per good HBM bit -15 to -25%.

title: Swiss cheese: two partial-good dies packaged as one standard DDR5 die
idea: Cheese with holes still sells by the block: bin dies with dead banks or mats, then package two complementary partial dies with a tiny bridge die that steers each bank address to whichever die has it working. The package is one standard 16/24/32 Gb DDR5 device, and dies scrapped today become product.
why: Bit supply: effective wafer output +5-10% at near-zero capex, the fastest supply lever.

title: Bunk beds: upper cell tier serves as lower tier's sensing reference
idea: Bunk beds stack two sleepers on one floor plan: layer-transfer a second single-crystal cell tier above the first array's capacitors and drop its bitlines to the same sense amps, so each sense amp compares a lower-tier bitline with the upper-tier bitline directly overhead (vertical folded pairing). Sense amps and periphery are shared, and the part is a standard DDR5/HBM die of twice the capacity.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and density: periphery per bit halves (~49% to ~33% of die area), ~1.7x bits/mm2, with folded-bitline noise immunity at open-bitline density.

title: Corrugated cardboard: rippled capacitor walls boost electrode area
idea: Corrugation adds surface: during the lateral-capacitor recess in a 3D stack, or the pillar etch in 2D, alternate etch and passivation cycles (Bosch-like scalloping) or a Si/SiGe sub-superlattice with selective recess give the electrode rippled walls before conformal ALD TiN/ZrO2/TiN. The cell footprint and the DDR5/HBM interface do not change.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): electrode area 1.5-2x, so Cs 7-9 fF at today's aspect ratio or today's Cs at AR ~40:1.

title: Leaf veins: backside copper grid straps wordlines, halving driver stripes
idea: Leaf veins feed every cell through branching: after thinning, add a low-resistance backside Cu grid that straps each Ru or Mo wordline every 64 cells through nano-vias, so wordlines can be 4x longer at the same RC. The die needs fewer, larger sub-wordline driver stripes, and DDR5 tRCD is unchanged.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7): sub-wordline driver area -50 to -75%, die about -8%; moving off tungsten wordlines also eases the China ~80% tungsten chokepoint.

title: Elevator counterweight: two tiers in series voltage domains recycle charge
idea: A counterweight falls as the car rises: run two cell tiers (or two stacked dies) in series voltage domains, the lower array between ground and mid-rail and the upper between mid-rail and supply, so the charge one tier dumps during precharge and restore becomes the supply charge of the other. A small on-die balancing regulator absorbs mismatch, and external rails and the interface stay standard.
why: Voltage floor and CV2 energy (fact 10): array charge drawn from the supply roughly halves, about -40% array activation energy.

title: Snowshoe: wide flat multilayer-plate capacitor replaces the tall cylinder
idea: A snowshoe spreads weight wide instead of sinking deep: replace the tall cylinder with ~20 alternating TiN and ZrO2/HfO2 horizontal plates deposited as a blanket stack, patterned once per cell, with odd plates tied to a storage post and even plates to a shared plate post by sidewall-selective recess and fill (MLCC-style). Only the capacitor module changes; the die and its DDR5/HBM interface do not.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): 4-6 fF from ~0.4 um of stack height with no high-AR hole etch and no pillar-collapse yield loss.

title: Shingled roof: TSV-free 3DS DDR5 via printed staircase edge traces
idea: Roof shingles overlap in steps: stack 4-8 DDR5 dies offset by 150 um in a staircase, and aerosol-jet or EHD-print 10-20 um silver traces down the exposed step edges to link each die's pads to the substrate in place of TSVs. The result is a standard 3DS DDR5 RDIMM device with an unchanged interface.
why: TSV tax (fact 6) for high-capacity server memory: no TSV area, keep-out or TSV yield loss; claim die area -6-8% and 3DS stack cost -20%.

title: Aquarium glass: core dies framed in glass carry HBM channels
idea: An aquarium holds its contents in a glass frame: embed each thinned, TSV-free DRAM core die in a glass frame with laser-drilled, Cu-filled through-glass vias, and stack the frames so the vertical HBM channel wiring runs through the glass around the dies, with short RDL fan-in to edge pads. The base die and the HBM3E/HBM4 interface do not change.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): core dies shed TSV area and keep-out (~10-15% of die) and become standard thin dies; glass is cheap and not a chokepoint.

title: Lottery drum: tier-randomized row placement re-keyed every refresh window
idea: A lottery drum reshuffles before every draw: in a 3D or stacked DRAM, a keyed permutation maps logically consecutive rows to physically non-adjacent rows in different tiers, and the key rotates every 32 ms window as refresh migrates rows through a small spare region. A hammer pattern cannot keep hitting the same physical neighbors, and the DDR5/HBM command set and timing are untouched.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): targeted multi-sided attacks lose physical adjacency; effective threshold up 10-100x with no controller change.

title: Zamboni: in-array microheater lines anneal leaky cells during self-refresh
idea: A Zamboni resurfaces the ice between periods: thread thin TiN heater lines under each mat, and during self-refresh or idle copy a mat's data to a neighbor, pulse the mat to ~150-200 C for milliseconds to de-trap the interface charges behind variable-retention and leakage-tail cells, then copy it back. The controller never sees it and keeps issuing normal REF commands.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): pruning the 13 fA tail 3-5x lets the die skip internal refreshes, cutting refresh energy (46 fJ/bit) and idle power by 10-20%.

title: Seesaw: vertical twin cell holds each bit across two tiers
idea: A seesaw rises on one side as it falls on the other: in a 3D die each bit is complementary charge on two cells stacked directly above one another on a vertical bitline pair, sensed differentially. The signal doubles and leakage is common-mode, so cheap tiers buy far longer retention behind a standard DDR5/LPDDR5 interface.
why: Refresh (fact 3) and capacitor wall (fact 1): 2x signal allows ~0.5x Cs per cell (shorter capacitors) and 4-8x longer retention; the 2x cell cost is paid in tiers.

title: Double helix: vertical bitline pairs twist between tiers, cancelling noise
idea: Like DNA strands swapping sides, true and complement vertical bitlines in a 3D array swap positions every 8 tiers through crossover vias, so coupling from neighbor bitlines and wordline steps lands equally on both and cancels in the sense amp. Vertical bitlines can then pack at minimum spacing without shields, inside a standard DDR5/HBM die.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2) and capacitor wall (fact 1): bitline coupling noise ~5x lower, allowing smaller sense signals (lower Cs) and ~20% tighter vertical bitline pitch.

title: Dating app: wafer-map matchmaking before wafer-to-wafer HBM stacking
idea: A dating app pairs compatible profiles: probe-test each DRAM wafer, store its defect map, and use an assignment solver to choose which wafers and which rotation (0/90/180/270) to bond wafer-to-wafer so bad sites land on bad sites. Dice the pre-bonded stacks into HBM core blocks with the standard HBM interface.
why: HBM yield (fact 6) and bonding throughput: W2W cost with yield loss near known-good-die D2W; claim stacking cost -30% and +10-15 points good-stack yield.

title: Thermostat: per-tier refresh skipping follows the HBM stack's thermal gradient
idea: A thermostat acts on local temperature: each HBM core die reads its own sensors and tier position (top dies run 5-15 C cooler than dies near the base) and quietly executes only a fraction of the controller's REF commands, for example 1 in 2 below 70 C. Commands and timing stay JEDEC; only internal energy drops.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3): 30-50% less refresh energy in cooler tiers, about 5-10% lower HBM idle power.

title: Coaxial cable: polymer-lined annular TSVs shrink keep-out to near zero
idea: A coax cushions its core with a soft dielectric: make each HBM TSV an annular Cu ring around a Si core with a 1 um BCB or parylene liner that absorbs the CTE stress, so transistors and mats can sit within ~1 um of the via instead of 5-10 um. TSV count and the HBM interface stay the same.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): keep-out area -80%, recovering ~5-8% of core-die area per bit.

title: Stilts: low-temperature wordline drivers built above the array, not beside it
idea: Stilts lift a house over its plot: build the sub-wordline drivers and column-select switches as <400 C oxide-semiconductor or laser-annealed poly-Si transistors in the BEOL directly over the cell array, connected down by vias, while Si sense amps and I/O stay below. Mat-edge driver stripes disappear, and externally it is still a standard DDR5 die.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7): removes ~15-20% of die area (driver and column-select stripes), about 20% more bits per wafer.

title: Chimney: micro heat-pipe thermal vias let HBM stacks grow taller
idea: A chimney draws heat straight up: etch dummy 10 um vias through the core dies at hotspots, aligned through the stack to the lid, and fill them with sealed two-phase micro heat pipes or a Cu-diamond composite. Bottom dies run 10-15 C cooler, so 16-24-high stacks fit the thermal envelope without changing the HBM interface.
why: Layer count capped by heat: +50% dies per stack at the same footprint and interface, and cooler dies need less refresh (fact 3).

title: Rubber stamp: nanoimprint replaces EUV on the periodic array layers
idea: A rubber stamp copies a pattern with no optics: because the cell array is perfectly periodic, pattern the capacitor-hole, bitline and active layers with jet-and-flash nanoimprint (one master, many replica templates), and keep EUV or DUV only for the irregular periphery. The die and its interface match standard DDR5.
why: Litho capital (fact 4): 3-5 of the 5-7 EUV layers move to imprint tools at ~1/5 the cost; claim wafer cost -10-15% and less dependence on the single EUV supplier.

title: Creme brulee torch: laser-grown single grains form monolithic cell tiers
idea: A torch caramelizes only the top: deposit amorphous Si over the finished periphery and lower array, then melt it with an excimer laser through a micro-Czochralski grain filter (a seed hole at each cell site), growing one single-crystal grain under each future access transistor at a BEOL thermal budget. Extra cell tiers stack above, and the die is still a standard DDR5 part at ~2x density.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2): near-single-crystal upper-tier transistors without wafer bonding; claim 2-4 tiers at <450 C for ~1.8x bits per die area.

title: Hourglass: pinched-waist vertical channel trims the leakage tail
idea: An hourglass narrows in the middle: shape each vertical access channel with a ~5 nm waist at the gate center (an oxidation-pinch step) and wide ends for low contact resistance, so the gate-drain edge field and the GIDL and trap-assisted leakage tail drop. The die skips most of the controller's REF commands internally while keeping DDR5 timing.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): 13 fA tail to ~2-3 fA; internal refresh rate 4x lower, refresh energy -50-75%.

title: Thermos flask: sealed vacuum gaps between wordlines block hammer coupling
idea: A thermos insulates with vacuum: after the buried wordlines are formed, recess the isolation dielectric between passing wordlines and neighbor active areas and seal it with a pinch-off cap, leaving vacuum gaps (k=1). Capacitive kick and charge migration from aggressor to victim fall, and the DDR5/HBM interface is untouched.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): coupling ~3x lower, aiming at a 3-5x higher flip threshold; lower wordline capacitance also trims wordline CV2 energy (fact 10).
